author: Great Lakes Wire
title: Detroit receives credit rating upgrades from S&P and Moody's in the same week
text:
The City of Detroit has received credit rating upgrades from both S&P Global and Moody’s Ratings, with Moody’s returning the city to the “A” category for the first time since 1999, Mayor Mary Sheffield announced on May 27. Moody’s elevated Detroit’s Issuer and General Obligation Unlimited Tax ratings to A3 from Baa1, while S&P raised its Unlimited Tax General Obligation bond rating to BBB+ from BBB.
“This great news from Moody’s and S&P validates our strong financial management practices and budget investment priorities,” said Mayor Sheffield. “We have shown that structural fiscal discipline can coexist with a commitment to uplifting and investing in our residents and our neighborhoods. These two rating increases also are a result of 12 years of sound, responsible budgetary choices made by the city department heads and Detroit City Council, alongside the expertise of our Chief Financial Officers.”
This marks Detroit’s twelfth consecutive year with an upgrade. The dual increase comes after only Moody’s upgraded Detroit in 2025. During its 2013 bankruptcy, Detroit’s credit rating fell to junk bond status but has since returned to investment grade through improved governance and consistent operating performance. The upgrades also coincided with a federal bankruptcy court judge closing its long-standing case with the city.
Moody’s stated, “The upgrade to A3 reflects the city’s strengthened financial resilience on par with A3 peers, supported by consistently solid operating performance, strong reserves, low leverage and good governance practices.” In its report, S&P cited “sustained strong financial performance and governance conditions” as well as improved ability to withstand economic uncertainty: “Detroit continues to bolster its financial resiliency and maintain solid operating performance, which will enable it to successfully weather the adverse effects of an economic slowdown, should one occur.”
Both agencies assigned a stable outlook for Detroit. S&P said this reflected confidence in Detroit’s long-term fiscal health due to robust planning efforts, substantial reserves, capacity for cost-cutting if needed, and continued fiscal discipline amid uncertain policy environments. Moody’s added that it expects stable financial performance supported by semiannual revenue estimating conferences and multi-year forecasting.
CFO Tanya Stoudemire said, “Reaching an A3 rating with Moody’s and a BBB+ rating with S&P stands as a testament to the rigorous structural infrastructure we have built across all city departments… By continuing our mission to maintain balanced budgets and robust cash reserves, we are ensuring long-term fiscal sustainability while simultaneously freeing up resources so the Sheffield administration can make meaningful investments that directly improve quality of life for all Detroiters.”
summary: “This great news from Moody’s and S&P validates our strong financial management practices and budget investment priorities,” said Mayor Sheffield. During its 2013 bankruptcy, Detroit’s credit rating fell to junk bond status but has since returned to investment grade through improved governance and consistent operating performance.
